content.text: An installed skill doesn't sit in Claude's context like CLAUDE.md. At startup Claude sees only a short listing: each skill's name and description. It reads the full SKILL.md when you run the skill or the task matches, and it opens the skill's other files only if the task needs them. That's progressive disclosure, and it's why a runbook belongs in a skill. But the listing and any skill you've used still cost context, so design for both.

A platform team keeps a 450-line incident runbook in CLAUDE.md: triage steps, rollback for twelve services, customer message templates. Someone suggests moving it into a skill. The lead says there's no point: "skills load into context just like CLAUDE.md." So every session, including one that renames a CSS class, starts with 450 lines of runbook. When they finally do move it, they paste all 450 lines into one SKILL.md and add forty skills from other teams in the same week. Two weeks later, during a real outage, Claude doesn't pick up the incident skill at all.
"Every installed skill's full instructions are in the context window all the time, just like CLAUDE.md." It sounds reasonable:

items.text: Skills are Markdown instructions in
.claude/
, exactly like
CLAUDE.md
and rules, which do load at startup.
Claude can pick a skill on its own, so it must already know what's inside, or so it seems.
Installing a plugin makes its skills "available" right away, which reads like "loaded".
Skills aren't free, and people have seen their context fill up after adding many.

content.text: The half-truth is the last point. Skills do cost context, but in stages, and a cost you don't pay at startup is a cost you can design around.
Three levels, loaded at three moments
: Claude "loads information in stages as needed, rather than consuming context upfront". An

items.text: The listing.

At startup, the name and description of every skill go into Claude's context. The description is what Claude matches your request against, so it has to say what the skill does and when to use it. Anthropic's Agent Skills overview estimates about 100 tokens per skill for this level.
The body.
When you type
/name
, or Claude decides the task matches the description, the SKILL.md body enters the conversation. Only then.
Everything else in the folder.
Reference files load only when Claude reads them. Scripts run, and only their output enters context; the code itself never does.

content.text: Anthropic's engineering post draws the conclusion: because files cost nothing until they're read, the amount of context you can bundle into a skill "is effectively unbounded".
Level 1 is cheap per skill, not free in total. In Claude Code the listing's budget scales at 1% of the model's

, and each entry's description is capped at 1,536 characters. Every skill name is always listed, but when the listing overflows, Claude Code drops descriptions, starting with the skills you invoke least. A skill without its description has lost the keywords Claude matches against, which is how the team's incident skill went quiet.
Two settings take a skill out of the listing on purpose.
keeps its description out of context entirely, and only you can run it, which suits skills with side effects such as
setting can set a skill you didn't write, such as one committed to a shared repo, to

Level 2 isn't paid once. The rendered SKILL.md enters the conversation as a single message and stays there for later turns, so every line is a recurring cost from then on, much like CLAUDE.md. Claude Code doesn't re-read the file, so instructions meant for the whole task should be written as standing rules. After

, Claude Code re-attaches each invoked skill but keeps only its first 5,000 tokens, within 25,000 tokens for all skills, dropping the oldest first. What's at the top of SKILL.md survives; what's at the bottom may not.
One file vs a skill folder
The runbook, first as one big SKILL.md and then split by when each part is needed:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
---
description: Incident runbook
---
# Triage
1. Check the dashboards ... (30 lines)
# Rollback, all 12 services
## billing ... (160 lines)
# Customer message templates
... (90 lines)
# Log query cookbook
... (120 lines)

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
---
description: Run an incident (triage, rollback, customer updates).
  Use when the user mentions an outage, an incident or an alert.
---
1. Run ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/recent-errors.sh and summarize
   the top five errors.
2. Find the failing service and the deploy just before it.
3. To roll back, read reference/rollback.md, that service only.
4. For a customer update, start from reference/comms.md.

content.text: The first version's description is too vague to reliably match "checkout is throwing 500s", and when it does load, all 400 lines ride along for the rest of the session. The second leads with the words people actually use, keeps only the steps, and points at the rest:

blocks.code:
incident/
├── SKILL.md              # steps and pointers, loaded when used
├── reference/
│   ├── rollback.md       # read only when rolling back
│   └── comms.md          # read only for a customer update
└── scripts/
    └── recent-errors.sh  # run, never read: only output in context

content.text: In SKILL.md, say what each supporting file contains and when to read it, so Claude can decide without opening all of them. The docs suggest keeping SKILL.md under 500 lines and moving detailed reference material to separate files.

blocks.title: More skills can mean fewer triggers

content.text: Every listed skill adds to context on every turn, used or not, and past the budget the least-used ones lose their descriptions. Run
to see each skill's cost and how often it's used, and turn off the ones nobody invokes.

items.text: At startup Claude sees each skill's name and description, not its instructions.
SKILL.md loads when you run the skill or the task matches; then it stays for the rest of the session.
Supporting files load only when read, and scripts cost only their output.
The listing has a budget: too many skills and the least-used lose the descriptions that make them trigger.
Lead SKILL.md with what matters most, because compaction keeps only the start.
